To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the radiation pressure produced by a quasiresonance optical photon flux can produce a very narrow velocity distribution peak in a time of 10–6 sec, which is a new effect that has not previously been observed.

the radiation pressure from oppositely directed optical photon fluxes produces a narrow peak in the velocity distribution function of an atomic gas and the position of the peak is governed by photon detuning.
the velocity of an atomic gas can be narrowed to a width smaller than γ/k in the field of quasiresonance optical radiation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the interaction between a gas and a laser field in the presence of an external magnetic field.
the study of the influence of radiation pressure on the atomic velocity distribution functions in the field of quasiresonantly interacting optical photon fluxes.
the study of the dynamics of the interaction between a laser beam and a gas.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the present work is a very interesting and valuable contribution in the field of laser cooling of atoms.
the radiation pressure is a useful tool in spectroscopy and that the use of radiation pressure for spectroscopic purposes is not limited only to the Doppler broadening.
this paper does not contain a single useful or new result.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a very narrow velocity distribution function can be obtained by using quasiresonance optical pumping in a gas.
the radiation pressure can be used to produce a very narrow atomic velocity peak and this peak may be shifted to the red or blue by changing the detuning.
the velocity distribution function of atoms in the field of a quasiresonance optical radiation flux may be narrowed to the width of ~10–3 cm/sec in a very short time (~10–6 sec).
The main takeaway from our work is that
the radiation pressure of oppositely propagating photons may be used to cool atoms to temperatures below the Doppler limit.
the velocity distribution function of an optically cooled gas may have a very narrow peak, whose width is much smaller than that of the thermal distribution.
the use of radiation pressure to cool a gas to temperatures below 1 mK is feasible.
